$comment: Ruling OC-8. Quotes behind every orchard calendar on plugins/orchard-calendars/*.json, keyed by the sourceKey a stage description, degree-day estimate or window names. Each entry is { sources: [{ url, publisher, date, quote, edition, page, note? }], gateEligible?, note? } from an https .edu or .gov page, quoted word for word. A degree-day estimate ships only from an entry with gateEligible true, which needs two agreeing sources from different hosts (ruling OC-5); where the guides disagree or only one gives a value, record both or the one with gateEligible false and say why in note. Sources from a page reader's extraction never count. No product, product class, rate, brand, PHI or REI is ever recorded here (OC-2). Empty until a local agent works docs/design/ORCHARD_CALENDAR.md 'Needs a local agent'; checked by apps/web/src/lib/plugins/orchardCalendar.sources.gate.test.ts.

sources.note: The bulletin's degree-day guidance (pp. 1-2, Tables 29 and 30) counts insect development from a trap biofix for these three moths. It gives no degree-day range for any bud stage, and the Penn State Tree Fruit Production Guide (AGRS-045, 2026-2027) is a paid download that was not read, so no stage has a second source. Per OC-5 no gddEstimate ships.

pome-va-2026.gdd.note: No bud-stage degree-day estimate ships (OC-5): VCE 456-419 gives degree days only for moth flights counted from a trap biofix, and Penn State AGRS-045 (2026-2027), the planned second source, is sold as a paid download and was not read. Stages are known only when the owner marks them.

sources.note: From 'Improved cultural practices for better summer disease management', printed with the third cover spray.

sources.quote: SJS crawlers appear now. Yellow crawlers may be detected by capturing them on a ring of black electrical tape tightly encircling a scale infested branch, sticky side out.

sources.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension, Virginia Tech, West Virginia University and University of Maryland Extension: 2026 Spray Bulletin for Commercial Tree Fruit Growers, VCE Publication 456-419 (ENTO-638)
sources.quote: In some years, primary scab and rust inoculum may be depleted by the time for the second cover spray. If this is the case and primary scab has been well controlled, the spray program should be aimed more at control of “summer diseases” including Brooks spot, sooty blotch, fly speck, and rots. If mildew is a problem, maintain mildew protection until shoot growth hardens off.

sources.quote: Tight Cluster: Applies only to apple. Blossom buds mostly exposed, tightly grouped, stems short.

sources.quote: In the spring, as the daily average temperature increases and early bud development begins mobilizing stored carbohydrates, the overwintering bacteria multiply and initiate new infections in bark tissues at about 90-96 cumulative degree days above 55˚F after green tip (approx. tight cluster to open cluster stage of spur bud development). Symptoms of these first infections won't be apparent until several weeks after bloom
sources.note: Only the stage and the fact are used. The degree-day figure is a single-source disease estimate, not a bud-stage estimate, and does not ship (OC-5).

sources.quote: Early detection of GFW is important. Tap tree limbs over sheet beginning at prepink. GFW larvae will curl up (grub-like) when dislodged from tree.

sources.quote: In spring, during the blossom period, examine the orchard floor for apothecia, the cup-shaped fungal structures that produce ascospores. Their presence should be considered a potential plant disease emergency.

sources.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension, Virginia Tech, West Virginia University and University of Maryland Extension: 2026 Spray Bulletin for Commercial Tree Fruit Growers, VCE Publication 456-419 (ENTO-638)
sources.quote: In spring, survey the orchard for blossom infection and prune out any cankers and infected shoots.

sources.note: Note to Table 13, Seasonal Activity of Peach Diseases.

sources.quote: As it happened in 2017, the Mid-Atlantic region experienced an unusually warm February that influenced bud swelling and infection by Taphrina deformans (leaf curl) earlier than normal.
sources.note: Note to Table 13, Seasonal Activity of Peach Diseases.

sources.quote: Prune correctly and at the proper time. Infection at pruning cuts is less frequent when pruning is delayed until spring. Delay pruning until the first forecasts of warm, dry weather.
sources.note: From the peach canker (Cytospora canker) discussion.

sources.quote: Apply at early leaf drop to protect the leaf abscission scars from fall infection and subsequent overwintering twig infection.

sources.note: Under FALL PRE-DORMANT SPRAY. Only the diseases and the leaf-drop timing are used; the product named here is left out (OC-2).

sources.quote: Optimal spray timings for oriental fruit moth control in apple and peach differ through the season and are based on accumulated DD from separate biofix dates established for each crop at the beginning of each season (See Table 30).
sources.note: The bulletin's peach degree days count oriental fruit moth from a trap biofix. It gives no degree-day range for any peach bud stage.

stone-fruit-va-2026.gdd.note: No bud-stage degree-day estimate ships (OC-5): VCE 456-419 gives degree days only for moth flights counted from a trap biofix, and Penn State AGRS-045 (2026-2027), the planned second source, is sold as a paid download and was not read. Stages are known only when the owner marks them.
